frameworks.name: LTV:CAC Automation Ratio Framework
frameworks.definition: The minimum acceptable ratio of lifetime gross profit to customer acquisition cost varies by the number of business functions (lead gen, conversion, delivery) that are automated vs. manual: all three automated = 3:1 minimum; two automated = 6:1; one automated = 9:1; none automated = 12:1+.

frameworks.name: 30-Day Cash Black Box
frameworks.definition: A presale model in which ad spend is made on day 0, leads close within 24 hours, and total cash collected from those customers within 30 days exceeds the ad spend, creating a self-financing loop that funds the business build-out before the doors open.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the business with the higher lifetime gross profit per customer will always outspend competitors in any paid attention auction, creating a legal advertising monopoly: a gym using his six-week challenge model collected ~$1,000 from each customer within 30 days versus the industry-standard ~$21, and could therefore spend 10x more per lead while remaining profitable, crowding out all competitors on every ad platform in that market.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Businesses competing on paid advertising platforms where spend is an open auction
Comparable customer acquisition cost (~$100 per customer regardless of model)
claims.mechanism: When both businesses pay roughly the same price per lead, the business that extracts more gross profit per customer can reinvest more into ad spend without going cash-flow-negative, eventually monopolizing available ad inventory and blocking competitors from reaching new leads.
bounded_by: Requires ability to actually deliver at scale once leads are acquired
Applies to markets with paid attention auctions; less applicable to purely organic or referral-only channels

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the minimum acceptable LTV:CAC ratio for a business where all three core functions (lead generation, conversion/sales, and delivery/fulfillment) are fully automated is 3:1; as manual labor replaces automation in each function, the required minimum ratio increases by 3x per manual step: two automated = 6:1, one automated = 9:1, none automated = 12:1 or higher.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Ratios represent minimum thresholds for sustainable scaling, not optimization targets
claims.mechanism: Manual labor at any step introduces ramp-up costs (new hires underperform for months), lumpy capacity constraints (converting from 5 to 6 salespeople tanks metrics temporarily), and higher per-unit delivery cost at scale — all of which compress the effective ratio and can push a 3:1 business into unprofitability during growth phases.

numbers.axis: LTV:CAC minimum ratio by number of automated business functions

anchors.region: All 3 functions automated (lead gen + conversion + delivery)

bounded_by: 3:1 threshold applies only when all three functions are automated — widely cited Silicon Valley rule of thumb, per Hormozi, is incomplete without this condition

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that customer acquisition cost (CAC) always rises over time as a business scales, regardless of platform, because CPMs increase as more competitors enter the market, and because scaling ad spend forces the algorithm to show ads to progressively less-interested audiences, requiring more impressions per conversion.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Paid advertising channels where spend is in real-time auction
Businesses scaling beyond initial warm or high-intent audience
claims.mechanism: Ad platforms rank audiences by predicted conversion probability; early buyers represent the highest-intent cohort. As spend scales, the algorithm must reach lower-probability audiences, requiring more ad impressions per conversion, which increases CPM-equivalent cost. Simultaneously, new competitors bidding into the same auction push CPMs up independently.
bounded_by: May not apply to businesses with compounding viral or referral coefficient that reduces dependence on paid cold acquisition

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that a business with a $5,000 LTV and $500 CAC (10:1 ratio) is a superior business to own compared to one with a $1,000 LTV and $200 CAC (5:1 ratio), even though the second business has a lower absolute CAC — because optimizing for the ratio of return on customer spend, not the absolute cost, determines how aggressively capital can be reinvested.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Both businesses have capital available to reinvest
Both businesses operate in paid acquisition channels
claims.mechanism: A higher LTV:CAC ratio allows reinvesting more dollars per customer acquired into the acquisition machine; the business with $500 CAC and $5,000 LTV can double spend and still achieve 10:1 return, while the $200 CAC / $1,000 LTV business achieves only 5:1 even at optimum — meaning the first business compounds faster at scale.

numbers.axis: LTV and CAC comparison across two business scenarios

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that most business owners misattribute poor growth to advertising methods (Facebook ads not working, outbound not working) when the actual constraint is their business model economics — specifically an insufficient LTV:CAC ratio that makes any paid acquisition channel unprofitable regardless of the method used.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: When LTV is lower than CAC, no advertising method can create a sustainable return — improving creative quality, targeting, or outreach tactics reduces cost per lead but not the structural gap between what customers are worth and what they cost to acquire. The root cause is model economics, not method execution.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the 30-day cash-collection window is the critical constraint for bootstrapped businesses because most small businesses can tolerate waiting 30 days for return on acquisition spend, credit cards provide interest-free float for exactly 30 days, and any payback period longer than 30 days requires either outside capital or acceptance of compounding cash-flow risk.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Bootstrapped businesses with no outside investors
Businesses relying on credit card float or personal capital for acquisition spend
claims.mechanism: Credit cards grant 30-day interest-free float, making 30 days the natural constraint on how long acquisition capital can be deployed before requiring return to reinvest. Longer payback periods require either external credit lines or accepting cash-flow drag that limits reinvestment velocity.

numbers.axis: Cash payback period and capital source

anchors.value: Interest-free using credit card float; tolerable for bootstrapped businesses
Requires external financing or cash reserves; adds compounding risk

bounded_by: VC-backed businesses can sustain much longer payback periods by artificially inflating cash via outside investment

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the back-of-napkin LTV calculation performed over an extended period (a full year of data) is often more accurate than monthly snapshots because annual averaging smooths out seasonal peaks and troughs, producing a more reliable picture of true customer lifetime economics.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Businesses with at least one full year of operating data
claims.mechanism: Monthly calculations capture the distortion of unusually good or bad months; annual aggregation averages across natural business cycles, reducing variance and providing a more stable basis for capital allocation decisions.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that high-value customers (those with high absolute purchase prices relative to their net worth) are less demanding per revenue dollar and less price-sensitive, meaning the LTV:CAC ratio expands as customer value increases — a business willing to spend more per customer typically wins a more profitable, less demanding customer base.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: High-ticket offers where purchase price is a small fraction of buyer net worth
claims.mechanism: Wealthier customers evaluate purchases as price-to-value ratios rather than absolute cost, reducing price objections; they also have fewer operational demands per dollar of revenue because the contract represents a smaller total share of their budget to manage.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that adding a downsell tier (a lower-priced version of the core offer for prospects who decline the full price) increases total revenue per marketing dollar spent by converting buyers who would otherwise leave without purchasing, but only if the downsell is priced and structured so that it does not cannibalize existing buyers who would have paid full price.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Requires the downsell to be positioned as a fallback, not the default offer shown to all buyers
Applies to businesses with a primary premium offer and identifiable price-sensitive segment that goes unconverted
claims.mechanism: Downsells monetize otherwise-lost prospects; if properly gated (only offered after full-price decline), they expand revenue per funnel without reducing average order value across buyers who would have converted at full price.
bounded_by: If downsell is the first option presented or too prominently featured, existing buyers migrate to it, reducing average revenue per customer and total LTV

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that the model (business economics and LTV:CAC ratio) is a durable competitive moat, while methods (specific advertising tactics, DM hacks, viral hashtags) are transient one-trick plays that competitors can copy; businesses that optimize for model beat businesses that optimize for method over any meaningful time horizon.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Methods are replicable immediately by any competitor once discovered; a better business model (higher LTV per customer) enables permanent outspending of all competitors in any shared advertising auction, independent of which specific method either party uses at a given time.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that businesses scaling with manual labor in their acquisition, conversion, or delivery functions will experience temporary but severe metric degradation each time they add new headcount — specifically, conversion rates and delivery quality will dip during ramp-up periods, meaning businesses operating near breakeven at 3:1 LTV:CAC will become unprofitable during every hiring event.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Businesses with manual (not automated) lead gen, sales, or delivery functions
Businesses operating near LTV:CAC minimums rather than with significant buffer
claims.mechanism: New hires in sales, marketing, or delivery underperform relative to seasoned staff for weeks to months; the business incurs their full compensation cost on day one while their output contribution accrues gradually. At 3:1 LTV:CAC, this ramp-up cost destroys the margin buffer and pushes the business cash-flow-negative during every growth event.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in his gym presale model (2010s), investing $5,000 in ad spend at $100/day generated enough customer prepayments within 30 days to finance the entire physical gym build-out — demonstrating that a sufficiently high LTV:CAC ratio allows a business to self-fund capital expenditures through customer acquisition rather than debt or equity financing.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Requires customer payment to be collected before delivery (presale model)
Requires LTV within 30 days to exceed CAC, producing positive cash each day
claims.mechanism: Daily ad spend of $100 produced 10 leads, closing 2 at $600 each = $1,200 revenue against $100 cost the same day. Compounding daily, the $5,000 initial capital grew to ~$100,000 within 30 days, funding equipment, flooring, signage, and full gym build-out without debt or investor capital.

anchors.value: $100/day → 10 leads → 2 closes at $600 each = $1,200 same-day revenue
~$100,000 in total sales, funding full gym build-out from $5,000 initial deposit

bounded_by: Required a presale model where customers paid before gym opened; not applicable to businesses that must deliver before charging

examples.text: When Alex Hormozi entered the gym industry, the standard model charged $21 for a 21-day trial, then attempted to upsell customers to a $99/month membership. The industry's customer acquisition cost was ~$100 per lead, meaning gyms paid $100 to make $21, and needed to convert 1-in-3 trial members to the $99 membership — yielding an effective CAC of ~$300 for a $99/month member who stayed an average of 6 months. Hormozi's competing model charged $600 upfront on day 1 for a six-week challenge, sold $200 of supplements within 48 hours, and pre-sold a year-long membership at week 3 for $2,000 — blending to approximately $1,000 per customer in the first 30 days. Both businesses paid roughly $100 per acquired customer in advertising. The gym with Hormozi's model could outspend the legacy gyms on every ad platform indefinitely, effectively purchasing all available advertising attention in any local market it entered.

Hormozi illustrates the downsell/upsell levers using a physical book as the example: raise the price (charge more per copy); lower COGS (negotiate bulk printing or shipping rates); upsell a hardback or audio + ebook bundle; cross-sell a second book on a different topic; add financing for higher-priced editions; downsell a digital copy to buyers who decline the hardback. He repeats the same exercise for a table: raise price, lower manufacturing cost, upsell a marble version, downsell a wood/plastic version, cross-sell matching chairs or table covers, add a warranty upsell, add financing. The point is that any business can identify at least five to seven levers to improve LTV within minutes of applying the framework.

practices.text: To calculate your CAC, take your total annual marketing and sales-related spending (advertising, sales commissions, marketing labor/contractors) and divide it by the number of new customers acquired in the same year.

To calculate LTV (lifetime gross profit), take total annual revenue divided by total active customers to get average lifetime revenue per customer, then multiply by your gross margin percentage (revenue minus cost of goods or delivery, divided by revenue).

Run the LTV/CAC improvement exercise on your business: (1) Can you raise price? (2) Can you decrease delivery cost? (3) Can you add an upsell? (4) Can you add a downsell for unconverted buyers? (5) Can you add a cross-sell? (6) Can you add financing? (7) Can you change payment collection terms to front-load cash? If you cannot rapidly answer all seven for your business, you do not understand your business model well enough.

To improve CAC, focus on: (1) improving your core offer's compelling nature; (2) producing more and higher-quality ad creatives with better hooks and winner remakes; (3) conversion rate optimization (split-testing landing pages, follow-up sequences, and sales scripts); (4) training the sales team if phone sales are used; (5) advertising on platforms or audiences with lower CPMs — but never optimize for lowest absolute CAC without also tracking LTV, because cheap leads are often low-quality customers.

For any business, identify your 30-day customer value (gross profit collected within 30 days of acquisition) and your CAC, and compare the two numbers before making any decision about marketing channels or tactics. If 30-day gross profit is less than CAC, fix the model before increasing ad spend.
